etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: だ (“to be”) + から (“because”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 代 (dai, “replacement”) + 名詞 (meishi, “noun”), as it stands in for a noun.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 原 (gen, “principle”) + 理 (ri, “theory”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived as compound of 可愛い (kawaii, “cute, adorable”) + がる (-garu, “feeling or thinking that way”, suffix applied to nouns and adjective stems to create a verb).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/adi/ → /ad͡ʑi/ → /aʑi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *anti.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 味 (MC mj+jH).
Also used in Old Japanese as 借音 (shakuon) kana for ⟨mi₂⟩.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nipa/ → */niba/*/ⁿba/ → /ba/
An alteration from Old Japanese 庭 (nipa), modern 庭(にわ) (niwa, “garden, yard”).
First cited to a text from 1275.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/djau/ → /d͡ʑoː/ ↔ /ʑoː/
From Middle Chinese 場 (MC drjang). Appears as a suffixing element in compounds since the early 700s. First cited as a standalone noun in the 太平記 (Taiheiki) of the late 1300s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 嫌 (iya, “despised”) + がる (-garu, “to act like”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 存(ぞん) (zon) + する (-suru, rendaku form する (zuru))

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨obi₁⟩ → */obʲi/ → /obi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ənpi.
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of 帯ぶ (obu, “to put something on the body”, transitive), following 四段活用 (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade conjugation”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 帶 (MC tajH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 平凡 (bjæng bjom, literally “even, flat + in every case”). Compare modern Min Nan reading pêng-hôan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kauun/ → /kɔːun/ → /koːun/
Probably from Middle Chinese compound 幸運 /幸运 (hɛng^X hjunᴴ, literally “lucky fortune”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)ばす (nobasu, “to grow, to spread”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 強 (kyō, “strengthen”) + 化 (ka, “cause to become”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 性 (MC sjengH, “nature of something, inherent quality”).
The goon, so the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 性 (MC sjengH, “nature of something, inherent quality”).
The kan'on, so a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/puri/ → /furi/
From Old Japanese.
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 振(ふ)る (furu, “to swing”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Related to 黒(くろ) (kuro, “black”), which see for more.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 変(か)える (kaeru), 代(か)える (kaeru) and 換(か)える (kaeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 王(おう) (ō) + 様(さま) (-sama)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of 痛(いた)む (itamu, “to cause pain, hurt”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese 真空 (MC tsyin khuwng).
First attested in the 懐風藻 (Kaifūsō) anthology of Sinitic poetry written by Japanese authors, compiled in 751.
The modern sense of vacuum is first attested in 1876.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 知 is a daiyōji replacing 智.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 空想 (khuwng sjang^X, literally “fictional, fabricated + think, thought”).
The sense of fantasy is first cited in Japanese to 1886, and probably reflects a Rangaku and Meiji era style of repurposing older terminology to translate unfamiliar Western concepts.
The Buddhist sense is older, and was borrowed into Japanese along with various Chinese Buddhist texts. This term is included in the 摩訶止観 (Maka Shikan), better known in English by its Chinese pronunciation, the Mohe Zhiguan, completed some time in the early 600s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 筋 (“muscle; tendon”) + 肉 (“flesh”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 組(く)む (kumu, “to assemble”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 組(くみ) (kumi, “class, group, team, set”) above. The kumi changes to gumi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sita.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 苦 (MC khuX, “suffering”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 議 (“discussion”) + 長 (“head”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 負(ま)ける (makeru, “to lose, to be defeated”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 透(す)く (suku, “to leave a gap”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 順 (jun, “order”) + 番 (ban, “numerical order”).
